papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: MEAL: Multi-Model Ensemble via Adversarial Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Often the best performing deep neural models are ensembles of multiple base-level networks. Unfortunately, the space required to store these many networks, and the time required to execute them at test-time, prohibits their use in applications where test sets are large (e.g., ImageNet). In this paper, we present a method for compressing large, complex trained ensembles into a single network, where knowledge from a variety of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) is distilled and transferred to a single DNN. In order to distill diverse knowledge from different trained (teacher) models, we propose to use adversarial-based learning strategy where we define a block-wise training loss to guide and optimize the predefined student network to recover the knowledge in teacher models, and to promote the discriminator network to distinguish teacher vs. student features simultaneously. The proposed ensemble method (MEAL) of transferring distilled knowledge with adversarial learning exhibits three important advantages: (1) the student network that learns the distilled knowledge with discriminators is optimized better than the original model; (2) fast inference is realized by a single forward pass, while the performance is even better than traditional ensembles from multi-original models; (3) the student network can learn the distilled knowledge from a teacher model that has arbitrary structures. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our MEAL method. On ImageNet, our ResNet-50 based MEAL achieves top-1/5 21.79%/5.99% val error, which outperforms the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practical Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity models into smaller, faster students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. The field has matured into a suite of complementary techniques — logits matching, feature and attention imitation, multi-teacher schedules, self-distillation, data-free synthesis, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search — and is applied across NLP, vision, speech, multimodal, and specialized domains. Empirical work shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover most teacher performance and enable deployment under strict compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints, but practical success depends on adapting objectives, data strategies, and student architectures to task and deployment constraints. Key open problems include distillation under data heterogeneity and privacy, preserving rare-token fidelity for sequence tasks, transferring robustness, and automating student architectures for diverse tasks.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Efficient Deep Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a foundational technique for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and graph domains. When applied thoughtfully — combining representational objectives, teacher-student co-design, task-aware compression, and appropriate data strategies — KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices while maintaining robustness and fairness. However, pitfalls arise from mismatches in inputs, teacher strength, data availability, and dataset biases; practical KD should therefore be integrated with complementary methods (e.g., architecture search, pruning, curriculum strategies, and data-generation) and with safeguards for ethical concerns.

papers_seen.author: Holt
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques that transfer information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving task performance. KD methods include matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, transferring relational structure, and leveraging multi-teacher or online schemes. KD is frequently combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and with data-aware strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical evidence shows KD often yields compact models that approach teacher performance across vision, language, ranking, and detection tasks, but its success depends on teacher–student alignment, data availability, optimization dynamics, and domain-specific constraints. Key open issues include robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-class or rare-token behavior, data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, and avoiding transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.author: Villa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically effective approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD provides multiple channels of transferable information (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals) and composes naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design). I argue KD should be treated as the backbone of compression pipelines: used by default as a first‑line strategy but applied in a context‑aware way, co‑designed with student architectures and data regimes, and paired with explicit mitigations for known failure modes such as distribution shift, rare-token degradation, privacy leakage, and teacher bias.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in model size and inference cost across vision and language tasks. When treated as a flexible toolkit—combining soft-target transfer, representation-level supervision, multi-teacher schedules, data- or privacy-aware synthesis, and integration with pruning/quantization/search—KD supports practical deployment under latency, memory, and data constraints. However, realizing its full potential requires careful teacher–student co-design, attention to data availability (including data-free and zero-shot approaches), and task- or architecture-aware objectives to avoid optimization and distributional failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression approaches seek to transfer useful information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, deployable student models while preserving performance. Research has expanded beyond matching final logits to include feature- and layer-level supervision, adaptive layer alignments, many-to-many mappings, task-aware filtering, teacher-free alternatives, data- and communication-constrained settings, and careful use of input-side techniques such as data augmentation. Empirical work shows these strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher accuracy across vision and language tasks, and practical pipelines combine pre-training of compact architectures with targeted distillation to improve downstream performance and deployment efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Promise, Mechanisms, and Responsible Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically effective approach for producing compact models that can be deployed under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. When treated as a flexible design paradigm rather than a single loss, KD supports multiple transfer signals (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals), integrates with complementary compression methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization), and adapts to task- and data-specific constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled signals, data availability (including data-free or synthetic strategies), and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and low-frequency behavior. A considered KD pipeline—combining softened logits, representational guidance, task-aware objectives, architecture-aware search, and careful data strategies—yields compact students that meet real-world deployment needs while mitigating common failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses high‑capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A broad family of distillation objectives—soft logits, intermediate representation alignment, attention- or relation-level transfer, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware variants—enables substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. Effective distillation is deployment- and capacity-aware: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data strategies (including synthetic or few-shot approaches), and integration with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Important open problems include data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine‑grained behaviors in language tasks, and maintaining robustness and fairness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Murillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster ones that remain useful in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD supports a wide range of operational needs: output- and feature-level transfer, data- and teacher-aware strategies, privacy-preserving distributed training, and task-adaptive compression. Realizing KD’s benefits in production requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacity, and how to combine distillation with complementary methods such as architecture search, pruning, task-aware layer selection, and synthetic-data techniques.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Juarez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students suitable for deployment under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. Across vision and NLP, KD methods extend beyond logit matching to include intermediate-representation imitation, attention and relational losses, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-constrained or data-free procedures. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation pipelines—especially when combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, or quantization—regularly yield compact models that recover much of the teacher’s performance, though open challenges remain around robustness, domain shift, fairness, and automated student design.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Adapt-and-Distill: Developing Small, Fast and Effective Pretrained Language Models for Domains
papers_seen.abstract: Large pre-trained models have achieved great success in many natural language processing tasks. However, when they are applied in specific domains, these models suffer from domain shift and bring challenges in fine-tuning and online serving for latency and capacity constraints. In this paper, we present a general approach to developing small, fast and effective pre-trained models for specific domains. This is achieved by adapting the off-the-shelf general pre-trained models and performing task-agnostic knowledge distillation in target domains. Specifically, we propose domain-specific vocabulary expansion in the adaptation stage and employ corpus level occurrence probability to choose the size of incremental vocabulary automatically. Then we systematically explore different strategies to compress the large pre-trained models for specific domains. We conduct our experiments in the biomedical and computer science domain. The experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves better performance over the BERT BASE model in domain-specific tasks while 3.3x smaller and 5.1x faster than BERT BASE. The code and pre-trained models are available at https://aka.ms/adalm.

papers_seen.author: Weber
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in model size, latency, and memory while often preserving predictive performance. Modern KD extends beyond soft-target (logit) matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, contrastive and relational signals, online or teacher-free co-training, and privacy- or communication-aware protocols. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data availability; remaining challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and reliable distillation when original data are limited or private.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. Over the past decade KD has matured from simple logits-matching into a multifaceted toolkit that includes soft-target supervision, intermediate representation alignment, attention and relation matching, data synthesis for data-free scenarios, online and federated distillation, and self-distillation. Empirical results show distilled students often approach teacher performance while yielding substantial gains in latency, memory, and deployability; however, practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of risks such as bias transfer, robustness loss, and privacy leakage. This synthesis summarizes core mechanisms, representative variants, theoretical insights, practical strategies, and open challenges to guide research and deployments in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels. KD variants transfer information at the output level (soft targets) and across internal representations (features, attention, relational signals), can operate with single or multiple teachers, and can be adapted to data-constrained, privacy-sensitive, or continual-learning settings. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign) and careful alignment of teacher and student (tokenization, pretraining, projector layers), KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. Remaining limitations include sensitivity to distribution shift, propagation of teacher errors or biases, preserving rare-class behaviors, and principled automation of trade-offs between fidelity and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central to deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans theoretical analyses of when and why distillation helps, practical algorithms for distilling logits, representations, and attention, techniques that require no original data, and adaptations for domains such as NLP, machine translation, and distributed training. Empirical work has shown KD can both accelerate inference and enable smaller models to approach or even exceed teacher performance in some settings, while recent advances address domain adaptivity, robustness, and teacher–student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Armstrong
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD transfers richer supervisory signals than hard labels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals) and composes naturally with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability or synthesis, and training schedules; open problems include reliable data-free distillation, preserving rare or safety-critical behaviors, robustness under distribution shift, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Gill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a System-Level, Practical Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best viewed not as a single trick but as a central, system-level toolkit for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student co-design, suitable data strategies (including synthesis or data-free protocols), and deployment-aware training schedules, KD yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities. However, its effectiveness depends on choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, and data availability; it also raises risks around transferring biases, losing rare-token behaviors, and underperforming under distribution shift. Treating KD as a first-line, flexible approach within a broader compression pipeline — rather than a one-size-fits-all cure — produces the most reliable outcomes for real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Multi-Strategy, Practical Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic and versatile approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a toolkit rather than a single recipe, KD can preserve much of a teacher’s predictive power while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques — representation matching, ensembling, architecture-aware compression, pretraining of compact students, and data-aware strategies — and when practitioners account for deployment-specific mismatches (domain shift, heterogeneous inputs, or limited access to data). Remaining challenges include robustly transferring rare or low-frequency information, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing data-free or privacy-preserving distillation that reliably generalizes under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, success hinges on what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate representations, or relational signals), how teacher–student mismatches and data constraints are handled, and how distillation is combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, architecture choices, and data-centric methods). Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can preserve most teacher performance under many conditions, but open problems remain in data-free and privacy-preserving settings, robust transfer under heterogeneity, and automated trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Practical Strengths, Limits, and a Pragmatic Prescription
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible set of methods for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Over a range of modalities and tasks, KD variants transfer richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive objectives), and they can be combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, or synthetic-data generation) to meet deployment constraints. KD reliably improves efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when teacher and student are properly aligned and when the distillation strategy matches data and system constraints; however, it is not a universal solution. Key limitations include sensitivity to teacher–student capacity mismatch, degraded transfer on low-frequency or domain-specific phenomena, and challenges when original training data are unavailable or under distribution shift. A pragmatic KD practice chooses appropriate distilled signals, co-designs student architectures, uses synthetic or adversarially generated data when needed, and evaluates robustness and fairness under realistic deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Explaining Knowledge Distillation by Quantifying the Knowledge
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a method to interpret the success of knowledge distillation by quantifying and analyzing task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts that are encoded in intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). More specifically, three hypotheses are proposed as follows. 1. Knowledge distillation makes the DNN learn more visual concepts than learning from raw data. 2. Knowledge distillation ensures that the DNN is prone to learning various visual concepts simultaneously. Whereas, in the scenario of learning from raw data, the DNN learns visual concepts sequentially. 3. Knowledge distillation yields more stable optimization directions than learning from raw data. Accordingly, we design three types of mathematical metrics to evaluate feature representations of the DNN. In experiments, we diagnosed various DNNs, and above hypotheses were verified.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a single teacher→student soft-label transfer into a broad toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across vision, language, and multimodal domains. Contemporary approaches extend logits matching to representation- and structure-aware objectives, multi- and continual-teaching schemes, task-aware layer selection, and combinations with pruning or architecture-level compression. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints but its success depends on design choices about what is transferred, how the student is supervised, data availability, and student capacity. Practical progress emphasizes representation matching beyond logits, careful layer- and channel-level alignment, and composing KD with other compression techniques; remaining challenges include robustness under distribution shift, data-free scenarios, and preserving fine-grained or safety-critical behavior.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of methods that transfers information from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost and memory while preserving task performance. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-label (logit) supervision to include intermediate feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on choosing appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacities and architectures, and handling data availability or provenance; open problems include principled teacher design, robust data-free approaches, preserving long-tail or safety-critical behaviors, and theoretical characterization of when particular knowledge sources help.

papers_seen.author: Lindsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core of Practical Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Pipeline Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining predictive performance. KD methods include soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free strategies. In practice KV succeeds when integrated into compression pipelines that also consider student architecture, pruning/quantization, data strategies, and explicit evaluations for robustness and rare-case behavior. However, KD has contextual limits driven by teacher–student mismatch, data availability or privacy constraints, optimization dynamics, and distribution shift; addressing these requires targeted design choices, careful signal selection, and complementary compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Olson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD comprises a family of techniques—matching teacher logits, aligning intermediate representations or attention patterns, leveraging multi-teacher or self-distillation schedules, and operating in data-constrained or data-free regimes. In practice KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and when design choices account for teacher–student capacity, data availability, and deployment constraints. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in theoretical understanding, robustness under distribution shift or imperfect teachers, transferring rare or fine-grained behaviors, and principled curricula for heterogeneous settings.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal signals from larger teacher models to smaller students. The KD toolkit spans softened-output (logit) supervision, representation- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and online or multi-teacher schedules; it interoperates with structural compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. When KD is co‑designed with student architectures and appropriate data strategies, it routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but its success depends on teacher quality, data availability (or synthesis), capacity and architecture mismatch, and explicit attention to robustness, rare-token or long‑tail behaviors, and privacy-sensitive constraints. Outstanding research directions include principled teacher selection and adaptation, reliable data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, faithful transfer of robustness and rare-token performance in language models, and scalable distributed or online distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Cameron
papers_seen.title: Well-Read Students Learn Better: On the Importance of Pre-training Compact Models
papers_seen.abstract: Recent developments in natural language representations have been accompanied by large and expensive models that leverage vast amounts of general-domain text through self-supervised pre-training. Due to the cost of applying such models to down-stream tasks, several model compression techniques on pre-trained language representations have been proposed (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). However, surprisingly, the simple baseline of just pre-training and fine-tuning compact models has been overlooked. In this paper, we first show that pre-training remains important in the context of smaller architectures, and fine-tuning pre-trained compact models can be competitive to more elaborate methods proposed in concurrent work. Starting with pre-trained compact models, we then explore transferring task knowledge from large fine-tuned models through standard knowledge distillation. The resulting simple, yet effective and general algorithm, Pre-trained Distillation, brings further improvements. Through extensive experiments, we more generally explore the interaction between pre-training and distillation under two variables that have been under-studied: model size and properties of unlabeled task data. One surprising observation is that they have a compound effect even when sequentially applied on the same data. To accelerate future research, we will make our 24 pre-trained miniature BERT models publicly available.

papers_seen.author: Schultz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a System-Level Primitive for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. When treated as a system-level primitive rather than a single loss term, KD can be adapted to data availability, deployment constraints, and student–teacher mismatch to produce compact models that retain much of teachers' performance. Practical application of KD involves choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention, relational signals), how to expose students to informative inputs (real, synthesized, or online predictions), and how to combine KD with complementary compression methods and privacy-preserving protocols. Despite strong empirical success, KD has known failure modes tied to teacher errors, limited data, and distribution shift that require targeted mitigations and principled design.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical, multi-strategy toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students in vision and natural language processing. KD methods transfer information at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention/relational signals) and are frequently combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Practical success depends on teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability or synthesis, and careful choice of distilled signals and training schedules; remaining challenges include data-free distillation, heterogeneity between architectures, robustness and fairness under compression, and preservation of rare behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Stewart
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a General-Purpose Compression Strategy for Deep Models: Evidence, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a specialized technique for transferring softened output distributions into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing and adapting deep models across domains (vision, language, multimodal, and generative models). Empirical results across tasks show that KD can preserve or even improve accuracy while substantially reducing model size and latency, and it can be combined with complementary strategies (pre-training, low-precision arithmetic, data synthesis, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints and privacy requirements. However, effective distillation requires attention to what is transferred (logits, internal representations, attention maps), how teachers and students are aligned (layer mapping, input alignment), and whether real data are available (data-free or adversarially guided generation). This paper synthesizes evidence from recent work to argue that KD, when applied with these considerations, is a reliable foundation for practical model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compressing and Deploying Large NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and flexible approach to compress large deep models so they can be deployed under latency, storage, and privacy constraints. By transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations from a high-capacity teacher to a smaller student, KD enables large pre-trained NLP models to be adapted, accelerated, and sometimes even improved for downstream tasks and specific domains. Effective KD requires careful design choices—how to match intermediate layers, whether to rely on data or synthesize surrogates, how to combine multiple teachers, and how to account for fairness and domain shift. When combined with complementary compression techniques, KD becomes a core component of production-ready model compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, distillation methods—ranging from matching teacher soft targets to aligning intermediate features or using data-free synthesis—enable substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical deployments combine distillation with architecture-aware choices (pruning, replacement, or search), multi-teacher or online schemes, and task-aware data strategies. Success depends on teacher quality, choice of transfer targets, data availability, and handling of mismatches; when carefully designed, distillation yields compact, robust models suitable for resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Scott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based signals, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data synthesis—has been developed and combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance in many vision and language tasks, while remaining sensitive to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, domain shift, and robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore co-design student architectures, distillation targets, and data handling strategies to achieve the best trade-offs for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Ramirez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, System-Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact student models that preserve much of a larger teacher’s accuracy while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. KD succeeds most reliably when treated as a system-level design choice rather than a single auxiliary loss: practitioners should choose what signals to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), align student and teacher architectures, incorporate complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and address data limitations through augmentation or data-free/federated strategies. KD has proven value across modalities but also carries risks — optimization difficulties, teacher errors propagated to students, and sensitivity to available data — that require explicit mitigation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Confidence-Aware Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is initially introduced to utilize additional supervision from a single teacher model for the student model training. To boost the student performance, some recent variants attempt to exploit diverse knowledge sources from multiple teachers. However, existing studies mainly integrate knowledge from diverse sources by averaging over multiple teacher predictions or combining them using other various label-free strategies, which may mislead student in the presence of low-quality teacher predictions. To tackle this problem, we propose Confidence-Aware Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (CA-MKD), which adaptively assigns sample-wise reliability for each teacher prediction with the help of ground-truth labels, with those teacher predictions close to one-hot labels assigned large weights. Besides, CA-MKD incorporates intermediate layers to stable the knowledge transfer process. Extensive experiments show that our CA-MKD consistently outperforms all compared state-of-the-art methods across various teacher-student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Adversarial Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has made remarkable progress in the last few years and become a popular paradigm for model compression and knowledge transfer. However, almost all existing KD algorithms are data-driven, i.e., relying on a large amount of original training data or alternative data, which is usually unavailable in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we devote ourselves to this challenging problem and propose a novel adversarial distillation mechanism to craft a compact student model without any real-world data. We introduce a model discrepancy to quantificationally measure the difference between student and teacher models and construct an optimizable upper bound. In our work, the student and the teacher jointly act the role of the discriminator to reduce this discrepancy, when a generator adversarially produces some "hard samples" to enlarge it. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed data-free method yields comparable performance to existing data-driven methods. More strikingly, our approach can be directly extended to semantic segmentation, which is more complicated than classification, and our approach achieves state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Efficient Transformer-based Large Scale Language Representations using Hardware-friendly Block Structured Pruning
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained large-scale language models have increasingly demonstrated high accuracy on many natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, the limited weight storage and computational speed on hardware platforms have impeded the popularity of pre-trained models, especially in the era of edge computing. In this work, we propose an efficient transformer-based large-scale language representation using hardware-friendly block structure pruning. We incorporate the reweighted group Lasso into block-structured pruning for optimization. Besides the significantly reduced weight storage and computation, the proposed approach achieves high compression rates. Experimental results on different models (BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT) on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks show that we achieve up to 5.0x with zero or minor accuracy degradation on certain task(s). Our proposed method is also orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained language models such as DistilBERT using knowledge distillation, since a further 1.79x average compression rate can be achieved on top of DistilBERT with zero or minor accuracy degradation. It is suitable to deploy the final compressed model on resource-constrained edge devices.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Beyond Dark Knowledge: A Practical Position on How and Why Knowledge Distillation Works for Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile toolkit for compressing large models and adapting knowledge across architectures, domains, and devices. Its effectiveness derives from multiple mechanisms: soft-target regularization that shapes student generalization, representation-level transfer that preserves structure beyond logits, and methods that remove dependence on the teacher's training data. However, KD is not a single monolithic recipe — optimization dynamics, teacher-student mismatch, and interactions with other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing or fairness constraints) materially affect outcomes. I argue that practitioners should treat KD as a collection of complementary approaches (logit regularization, feature mimicking, contrastive alignment, data- or generator-based sample synthesis, and adaptive teacher selection) and choose combinations appropriate to their constraints (data availability, privacy, compute, heterogeneity). This perspective explains why simpler or even teacher-free approaches can match standard KD in many settings, and why representation- and adaptation-oriented variants expand KD’s applicability to domain adaptation, federated and graph models.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default Compression Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP: Rationale and Practical Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the default, first‑line strategy for compressing large neural models in deep learning and NLP because it provides flexible, task‑aware transfer channels that preserve predictive behavior while enabling complementary structural compression. KD excels when combined with architecture-aware design, representation-level alignment, and data strategies that address limited or private training data. A practical KD-first pipeline—selecting appropriate transfer signals, applying task-aware layer mappings, leveraging data-free or augmentation methods when needed, and composing KD with pruning/quantization—yields robust, high-compression students suitable for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Mechanisms, and Constraints
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for compressing large deep models into smaller, efficient students suitable for production. KD methods span soft-label transfer, representation- and layer-level matching, adversarial and privacy-aware variants, and meta- or teacher-adaptive strategies. When combined with appropriate pre-training, architecture-aware adapters, and task-aware objectives, distillation yields compact models that approach teacher performance under realistic compute, data, and deployment constraints. However, outcomes depend on teacher–student compatibility, what signals are distilled, and whether robustness or privacy guarantees are required.

papers_seen.author: Dominguez
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as a System-Level, Context-Dependent Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Its value arises from flexible choices about what and how to transfer (logits, features, relational signals), how to expose students to informative inputs (real, synthesized, or online signals), and how to combine distillation with architecture and numerical compression. However, distillation is not automatic: teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability or privacy constraints, and deployment targets (latency, memory, robustness, fairness) materially affect outcomes. Viewing distillation as a system-level primitive — one part of a broader compression and deployment pipeline — yields better, more reliable trade-offs between efficiency and retained capability.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- or resource-constrained settings. Across NLP and broader deep learning applications, researchers have developed logit-based distillation, feature- and attention-level mimicking, ensemble- and multi-teacher schemes, task-adaptive compression, and data- or teacher-free variants. These methods trade off compute, memory, and sometimes robustness or fairness, and are often complementary to pruning and architecture search. Practical adoption favors combinations of pretraining, targeted distillation objectives, and adaptations to mismatches between teacher and student (e.g., inputs or architecture).

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information from teacher models. KD encompasses a family of techniques — matching teacher logits (soft targets), aligning intermediate features or attention maps, online or mutual distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants — that are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance in vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality and specialization, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and optimization choices; naive distillation can propagate teacher errors or fail under strong teacher–student mismatch. Practical pipelines therefore select distillation signals and schedules appropriate to task and deployment constraints, often pairing KD with complementary compression techniques to trade compute and size for modest predictive degradation.

papers_seen.author: Conner
papers_seen.title: Distilling Task-Specific Knowledge from BERT into Simple Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: In the natural language processing literature, neural networks are becoming increasingly deeper and complex. The recent poster child of this trend is the deep language representation model, which includes BERT, ELMo, and GPT. These developments have led to the conviction that previous-generation, shallower neural networks for language understanding are obsolete. In this paper, however, we demonstrate that rudimentary, lightweight neural networks can still be made competitive without architecture changes, external training data, or additional input features. We propose to distill knowledge from BERT, a state-of-the-art language representation model, into a single-layer BiLSTM, as well as its siamese counterpart for sentence-pair tasks. Across multiple datasets in paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification, we achieve comparable results with ELMo, while using roughly 100 times fewer parameters and 15 times less inference time.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. A rich set of distillation techniques—including soft-target/logit matching, intermediate representation and attention alignment, adversarial and relational objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and data-synthesis or data-free approaches—has been applied across NLP, vision, graphs, ranking, and healthcare. Practical compression usually pairs distillation with architecture-aware strategies (pruning, quantization, or search) and careful design choices about what, how, and when to transfer knowledge; success depends on teacher quality, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and attention to robustness and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Alexander
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and System-Level Guidelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. While KD can preserve much of a teacher’s predictive power and support deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, its success depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention), teacher–student compatibility, available data, and complementary compression techniques. A pragmatic stance treats KD as the central first-line tool in a broader compression pipeline, combined with pre-training of compact architectures, representation alignment, and targeted interventions for robustness, fairness, and data-limited or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Dunn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — softened output distributions, intermediate feature or attention alignment, relational losses, and synthetic-data supervision — and are commonly combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical results across vision, language, graph, and federated settings show KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, available data, and deployment constraints. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a central, configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a single, universal algorithm.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a diverse toolkit—intermediate representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-teaching schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants—and is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical application requires careful teacher–student co‑design, data strategies appropriate to deployment constraints, and targeted mitigations for known failure modes such as distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and inadvertent transfer of undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Contemporary Approaches and Insights in Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer useful information from larger, more expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, deployable models. Research spans theoretical analyses of what is transferred, architectural and loss-design strategies to improve feature and output matching, specialized teacher–student training regimes (including multi-teacher and student-aware teacher training), online and federated distillation for large-scale or privacy-sensitive settings, and structural compression strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing memory and compute. Applications include image models, generative models, question-answering systems and multi-task natural language understanding, with methods tailored to domain constraints such as heterogeneous device capabilities and privacy requirements.

papers_seen.author: Tran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques transfer behaviors of large models into smaller, more efficient models by supervising students with information derived from teachers (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention, or synthetic labels). Empirical results across vision, speech, and language show that carefully designed distillation pipelines can preserve much of a teacher’s performance while reducing size and latency. Effective practice combines choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data strategies (including augmentation or synthesis), and complementary structural compression. Remaining challenges include handling imperfect teachers, limited or private data, robustness and out-of-distribution behavior, and principled automation of trade-offs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Wagner
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or multi-modal models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural insights. Research has developed diverse KD variants—soft-label distillation, internal and layer-wise imitation, task-aware filtering, data-free distillation, and architecture-search guided compression—each addressing optimization, data availability, or deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work highlights trade-offs between matching teacher outputs and student generalization, the value of pre-training compact models, and the importance of choosing what and how knowledge is transferred to maximize downstream task performance while meeting resource limits.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer knowledge from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Across modalities and tasks, KD has evolved from simple soft-target matching to a toolkit that includes intermediate-feature alignment, attention and relational transfer, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data- or privacy-aware variants. Practical deployments typically combine KD with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, and data strategies; remaining research challenges include robustness under distribution shift, preserving low-frequency or rare behaviors, privacy leakage, and principled automation of teacher/student design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teacher models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels. Over the past decade KD has expanded from softened-logit matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, layer-wise mapping, multi-teacher and online schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture co-design) and careful data and teacher–student design, KD routinely yields substantial inference and memory savings while retaining much of teacher performance. Outstanding challenges include reliable distillation without original data, robustness under domain shift, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and avoiding transfer of undesirable biases or privacy leaks.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.
