papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable, practical approach for shrinking large deep models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their predictive power. KD encompasses logit/soft-target transfer, intermediate-representation and attention matching, and online or multi-teacher variants; when combined with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and care about data and optimization, KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. However, KD is context-dependent: its success requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability, pretraining, and robustness and fairness constraints, so it functions best as a central component within a larger, deployment‑aware compression pipeline rather than as a single universal recipe.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher networks into smaller, deployable student models by transferring information richer than hard labels alone. While KD routinely produces compact models that approach teacher performance in many settings, open challenges remain around domain shift, long-tail behavior, reliable data-free distillation, and automated student design for target resource budgets.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applicable technique for producing compact models from larger teachers. Its strength lies in enabling favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks, while its primary risks arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or unavailable data, and distribution shift. A pragmatic approach treats KD as the backbone of hybrid compression systems: pick distillation signals that match student capacity and task complexity, combine KD with other compression methods, and adopt data- and evaluation-driven safeguards for robustness, privacy, and long-tail behavior.

papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques transfer information from larger or more informative models (teachers) into smaller or more efficient models (students). Research across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks has developed multiple KD objectives (soft-label matching, intermediate layer alignment, contrastive/representation losses), training regimes (offline teacher-student, online co-training, meta-learned teacher updates), and architecture-aware compression strategies (channel-wise attention, task-adaptive architecture search). Empirical and theoretical work highlights tradeoffs between bias and variance introduced by soft targets, the value of pre-training compact models before distillation, and the importance of data and augmentation choices for effective transfer. Emerging large-scale and privacy-aware deployments leverage online and federated distillation variants to reduce communication and improve reproducibility, while new approaches aim to make teachers more student-friendly or distill internal representations rather than only outputs. Key open challenges include matching representational structure across heterogeneous architectures, choosing what and when to distill, and scaling methods to very large datasets and distributed settings while preserving privacy and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core of Model Compression: A Pipeline‑Oriented, Context‑Sensitive Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the practical core and first‑line strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students, but only when embedded in a carefully designed pipeline. KD’s value comes from its flexibility — it can transfer soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure, and be applied offline, online, or with synthetic/data‑free inputs — and from its ability to compose with pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and data strategies. Yet KD is not a universal remedy: outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality and suitability, student capacity and architecture, availability and domain match of data, and explicit handling of robustness, fairness, and privacy. The recommended stance is pragmatic: prioritize KD as the core compression tool, combine it with complementary structural and data techniques, adopt teacher‑aware and student‑aware design (including meta‑teaching and targeted sample strategies), and evaluate compressed models under realistic deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal signals from larger teacher models to smaller students. The KD toolkit spans softened-output (logit) supervision, representation- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and online or multi-teacher schedules; it interoperates with structural compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. When KD is co‑designed with student architectures and appropriate data strategies, it routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, but its success depends on teacher quality, data availability (or synthesis), capacity and architecture mismatch, and explicit attention to robustness, rare-token or long‑tail behaviors, and privacy-sensitive constraints. Outstanding research directions include principled teacher selection and adaptation, reliable data-free and privacy-preserving distillation, faithful transfer of robustness and rare-token performance in language models, and scalable distributed or online distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that the students retain much of the teachers' performance while meeting resource, latency, or privacy constraints. KD methods include matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations or attention, synthesizing surrogate training data when original data are unavailable, and deploying progressive or ensemble-based strategies. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search) and training-time strategies (curricula, online distillation, or federated protocols) to balance efficiency and accuracy. Despite strong empirical success across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and designing principled objectives and curricula that preserve robustness and task-specific inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression — Powerful but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep learning and NLP models into smaller, deployable students. KD provides flexible supervision signals (soft targets, intermediate features, attention patterns) that enable substantial reductions in model size and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability, and task specificity. Realistic deployment therefore requires combining KD with complementary strategies (task-aware layer selection, architecture search, data augmentation or synthesis, multi-teacher schemes, and privacy-aware mechanisms) and evaluating tradeoffs under the target constraints.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central model-compression approach that trains compact student models to emulate larger teacher models so that inference cost, memory, and deployment barriers are reduced while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive behavior. Research has produced a family of distillation objectives (soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational losses), training regimes (offline, online, self-distillation, multi-teacher), and system-level integrations (pruning, structured sparsity, quantization, and architecture search). Empirical studies show well-designed distillation pipelines commonly recover a large fraction of teacher performance and sometimes improve generalization, but success depends on what knowledge is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints. Practical use therefore combines algorithmic choices with architecture-aware compression and data strategies tailored to the task and environment.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques has been developed—matching softened logits, aligning intermediate representations or attention, using multi-teacher or online co-training schedules, and synthesizing or augmenting data for training students. KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data alignment, and training dynamics. Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, progressive module replacement) and must address open challenges including heterogeneous or federated settings, data scarcity or privacy constraints, robustness under distribution shift, and preservation of low-frequency or domain-specific signals.

papers_seen.author: Bright
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a heuristic into a practical, multi-purpose toolkit for compressing large models while preserving performance across domains and modalities. KD enables deployment of powerful models on resource-constrained devices, supports domain adaptation, helps preserve privacy, and can be adapted to architectures ranging from transformers to GANs and GNNs. Complementary techniques — e.g., architectural replacement, data augmentation, multi-teacher schemes, and precision reduction — expand KD’s effectiveness. However, KD’s success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, internal representations, relations) and on availability or synthesis of appropriate data. The balance of method and setting determines whether KD yields compact models that meet real-world constraints without unacceptable loss of fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Short
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Line, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, practical starting point for compressing large models because it provides flexible, task‑aware mechanisms to transfer behavior from high-capacity teachers to efficient students. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute when combined with targeted design choices. However, its success depends on what signals are distilled, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and domain constraints; therefore KD must be integrated into a broader, context‑adapted compression pipeline rather than used as a blind one‑size‑fits‑all fix.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a multifaceted approach for producing smaller, faster models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD operates through multiple knowledge channels (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and ensemble consensus) and is commonly combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture redesign. Practical use of KD requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data provenance (including data-free or online synthesis when original data are unavailable), and targeted interventions to avoid propagating teacher errors or losing rare-token and domain-specific behaviors. While KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision, language, and graph tasks, its effectiveness is context dependent and benefits from integration into broader, task-aware compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are a widely adopted toolkit for producing smaller, faster models that retain much of the accuracy of larger teachers. Research across vision and language characterizes KD as a family of methods—transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, relational structure, or training signals via specialized curricula or online exchanges—and shows that KD integrates naturally with pretraining, architecture design, and deployment-aware strategies. Practical success depends on matching the choice of knowledge (what to transfer), the teacher-student pairing (capacity and architecture), available data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and optimization curricula to the target task and constraints. While KD routinely yields substantial runtime and memory gains with modest accuracy loss, open challenges remain in handling domain shift, rare-token transfer in NLP, optimization mismatch, and large-scale or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Oconnor
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, multifaceted approach for converting large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher performance. KD operates through multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps), integrates with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and adapts to constrained settings via data-free or privacy-aware protocols. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its success depends on careful teacher–student co‑design, data strategies, and explicit handling of robustness, rare-case behaviors, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and pragmatic framework for compressing large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or more private models across modalities and tasks. When applied thoughtfully — by matching outputs, intermediate representations, training dynamics, or ensembles — KD can preserve or even improve task performance while enabling low-latency inference, reduced memory/compute, and new deployment modes (e.g., federated, data-free, or low-precision). However, distillation is not automatic: design choices about what to transfer, when to transfer, and how to align teacher and student matter for robustness, domain shifts, and rare-token behavior. I argue that best practice combines representation-aware objectives, selective or collaborative teaching strategies, and deployment-aware constraints (privacy, communication, numeric precision) to realize the full benefits of distillation in NLP and other deep learning settings.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Bruce
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone—ranging from softened logits to intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure—and can be configured in offline, online, ensemble, or data-constrained regimes. When paired with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and attention to teacher–student compatibility, data provenance, and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest loss in predictive performance. Nonetheless, its effectiveness depends on design choices about what and how to transfer, data availability or synthesis, and explicit evaluation of robustness, fairness, and long-tail behaviors; these remain active research and engineering challenges.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: The Central Role of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach to compressing large neural networks for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Beyond simple model-size reduction, KD enables transfer of inductive biases, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving distributed training, data-free and zero-shot compression, and the transfer of adversarial robustness. Combining logit-based distillation with feature-level mimicking and carefully chosen regularization yields high-quality small models that remain competitive on downstream tasks in NLP and broader deep learning applications.

papers_seen.author: Hughes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core for Compression — Essential but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and effective method for producing compact neural models from large teachers, yielding favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP. However, KD alone cannot guarantee robust, deployment-ready compression: practitioners must address teacher–student capacity alignment, pre-training of compact architectures, choice of distilled signals (logits, intermediate features, attention), data provenance and augmentation, and the use of complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). When KD is treated as a central system-level primitive and combined with targeted interventions, it produces the most reliable compressed models for real-world deep-learning and NLP deployments.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression strategies have become central tools for shrinking large pretrained models into efficient deployable networks while preserving much of their performance. Methods range from transferring final-logit 'dark knowledge' to matching intermediate representations, attention maps, or feature distributions; from engineering compact student architectures to progressively replacing modules inside a single model. Applications span vision, speech, generative models, and NLP (including BERT compression and non-autoregressive translation), and extensions address scenarios with no access to original training data or heterogeneous, federated settings. Key trade-offs involve accuracy vs. size/latency, robustness and fairness, and the distributional assumptions needed for effective transfer. Important open problems include principled understanding of when and why distillation helps, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and reliably transferring robustness and inductive biases to small models.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Bounded Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, and natural language tasks. KD techniques — from logits matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, multi-teacher schedules, adversarial and data-free variants — enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of a teacher's performance. However, realizing these gains in practice requires task- and student-aware design choices, attention to data and privacy constraints, and explicit strategies to mitigate transferred fragilities. KD is therefore an essential tool in the compression toolbox, but not a universal remedy: careful method selection and evaluation under deployment constraints determine success.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Multi‑Strategy Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is most useful when treated as a system-level, context-sensitive toolkit rather than a single loss term. Properly designed distillation pipelines combine multiple forms of transferred knowledge (soft targets, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals), teacher–student co-design, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. However, distillation is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility, student capacity, data provenance (including options for data-free distillation), and explicit evaluation of robustness, rare-token fidelity, and fairness. A pragmatic research and engineering agenda focuses on matching distillation signals to student capacity, designing student-friendly teachers, integrating online and multi-teacher regimes where appropriate, and developing reliable data-free or privacy-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, more efficient students while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Across vision and language tasks, KD has evolved from simple soft-label transfers to a rich family of techniques including internal representation matching, attention- and channel-guided supervision, multi-teacher and ensemble signals, data-free and augmentation-driven methods, and architecture-aware transformations. Practical deployments combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search and must balance transfer of useful teacher information against risks such as propagating teacher errors or overfitting under limited data. The field continues to refine what teacher knowledge to transfer, how to synthesize or augment training data when it is unavailable, and how to align heterogeneous teacher–student architectures for robust, resource-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Tucker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, broadly applicable family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of their predictive power. KD enables large gains in inference speed, reduced memory footprint, and practical deployment under latency, compute, and privacy constraints. However, straightforward distillation can transfer undesirable properties and can underperform when data is limited or teacher–student mismatches are large. To realize KD's full potential practitioners should combine soft-target transfer with representation matching, targeted data augmentation or data-free synthesis, careful teacher design (including ensembles or student-aware teachers), and explicit robustness or privacy-aware objectives. These combined practices produce compact models that are accurate, efficient, and more robust for real-world NLP and deep-learning deployments.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that compresses large teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, KD methods include matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate features or attention maps, and using multi-teacher or data-free strategies. Practical pipelines combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Distillation often preserves much of a teacher’s performance but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and careful design of what and how knowledge is transferred.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Issues
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from pre-trained teachers. The approach spans soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-representation and attention alignment, layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free workflows. Empirical results show KD often recovers much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and optimization protocols. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors, maintaining robustness and fairness under distribution shift, and operating when original training data is limited or unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression encompass methods that transfer information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, deployable models (students), or otherwise reduce network size while retaining performance. Approaches range from matching final predictions to aligning intermediate representations, and they address practical constraints such as limited data, privacy, device heterogeneity, and robustness. Recent work spans algorithmic mechanisms (soft targets, layer mapping, adversarial sample synthesis), application-specific pipelines (BERT compression, non-autoregressive translation, task-adaptive models), and theoretical interpretations that link distillation to regularization. This synthesis summarizes core techniques, practical extensions, and open challenges reported in recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Sheppard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Patterns, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Over the past decade KD has evolved from matching softened output distributions to a rich toolkit that also includes intermediate-representation alignment, attention- and relation-based objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free training strategies. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD routinely produces compact models that retain much of a teacher’s predictive power. Important practical challenges remain, including robust transfer under distribution shift, preserving rare or domain-specific behavior (especially in NLP), and principled, privacy-aware distillation when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the default first‑line strategy for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students, provided it is applied as a context‑aware toolkit rather than a single recipe. When implemented with attention to what form of knowledge is transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or data synthesis), KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade‑offs in vision and language tasks. At the same time, KD has failure modes — including teacher–student mismatch, sensitivity to data and optimization dynamics, risk of transferring undesirable behaviours, distribution shift, and privacy concerns — that must be mitigated through careful design, validation, and integration with other compression and robustness techniques.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Channel Distillation: Channel-Wise Attention for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge from the data learned by the teacher network to the student network, so that the student has the advantage of less parameters and less calculations, and the accuracy is close to the teacher. In this paper, we propose a new distillation method, which contains two transfer distillation strategies and a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy is based on channel-wise attention, called Channel Distillation (CD). CD transfers the channel information from the teacher to the student. The second is Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD). Unlike Knowledge Distillation (KD), which allows the student to mimic each sample's prediction distribution of the teacher, GKD only enables the student to mimic the correct output of the teacher. The last part is Early Decay Teacher (EDT). During the training process, we gradually decay the weight of the distillation loss. The purpose is to enable the student to gradually control the optimization rather than the teacher. Our proposed method is evaluated on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet, we achieve 27.68% of top-1 error with ResNet18, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, we achieve surprising result that the student outperforms the teacher. Code is available at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Bishop
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core for Compression — Powerful but Insufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven toolkit that forms the practical core of many model-compression pipelines in deep learning and NLP. KD reliably improves accuracy–efficiency trade-offs by transferring soft targets, intermediate representations, and relational signals from large teachers to smaller students; however, real-world compression requires coordinated attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability and provenance, robustness and fairness, and the complementary use of architectural and low-level compression techniques. Framing KD as a system‑level primitive and combining it with targeted interventions produces the most reliable, deployable compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels. Practitioners use a spectrum of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and training paradigms (offline, online, multi-teacher, and data‑free) together with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation) to meet latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often preserve most teacher performance while substantially reducing compute, but success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability or synthesis strategies, alignment of internal representations, and optimization choices. Important open issues include reliable distillation without original data, preserving robustness and fairness under compression, and principled criteria for selecting distillation signals and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Morales
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer knowledge from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Practical deployments typically combine KD with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, and data strategies; remaining research challenges include robustness under distribution shift, preserving low-frequency or rare behaviors, privacy leakage, and principled automation of teacher/student design.

papers_seen.author: Estes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Across NLP, speech, vision, and recommendation systems, KD reduces inference cost and memory, enables deployment on constrained devices, and can transfer specialized capabilities when paired with appropriate data and training choices. Its effectiveness depends on what is distilled (soft targets, intermediate features, relational signals), the availability and synthesis of training data, and teacher–student design; complementary compression tools and safeguards addressing bias, privacy, and distributional mismatch are often required for robust, real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Understanding and Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. It encompasses soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and training-time adaptations that account for student capacity and deployment constraints. In practice KD is combined with complementary methods (architecture search, pruning, quantization, data augmentation, and data-free synthesis) to meet latency, memory, or privacy requirements. KD is effective across vision, language, generative models, and view- or modality-specific tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student compatibility, available data, and careful choice of distillation objectives and schedules; open challenges remain in robustness, rare-token behavior, fairness, and theoretical guarantees.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Complementary Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, flexible route to compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher’s capability. Across vision, speech, and language tasks, variants of KD — including multi-teacher schemes, internal-representation matching, self-distillation, many-to-many layer mapping, and data-free approaches — have shown that distilled students can approach or even match teacher performance. KD is also complementary to pruning and quantization, enabling stacked compression pipelines that meet strict hardware constraints. I argue KD should be a first-line technique for model compression in deep learning and NLP, applied in combination with other resource-aware methods and chosen variants adapted to data availability and task structure.

papers_seen.author: Brooks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Contexts, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, broadly applicable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD methods include soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate-representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-aware or data-free variants. When KD is co-designed with student architectures, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), it routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. However, KD’s effectiveness is context-dependent: success requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, availability and provenance of data, and explicit handling of robustness, fairness, and distributional-shift risks. Treating KD as a central, system-level tool—rather than a single recipe—maximizes its practical benefits while making its limitations manageable.

papers_seen.author: Serrano
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A variety of distillation objectives and training regimes have been developed (logit or soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive losses, self-distillation, multi-teacher curricula, and data- or privacy-aware variants). In practice, distillation is most effective when paired with architecture-aware student design, appropriate data strategies (including synthetic or public-data surrogates when original data are unavailable), and complementary compression techniques such as pruning and quantization. Key open challenges remain in reliably transferring rare or long-tail behaviors, preserving robustness and fairness after compression, and designing principled teacher–student curricula across heterogeneous architectures and data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Theory, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. The field comprises a family of methods that transfer different forms of information—from soft logits to internal representations, attention maps, and relational structure—and integrates naturally with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Success depends on choosing what to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities and architectures, managing data availability (including data-free or federated setups), and designing appropriate optimization curricula. While KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, important limitations remain around teacher–student mismatch, domain shift, rare-token preservation in NLP, and robustness under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Strategy for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured from a niche compression trick into a unifying strategy that addresses model size, inference latency, domain shifts, multimodal transfer, privacy, and training efficiency. By transferring supervisory signals, intermediate representations, or relational structure from larger or more capable systems, KD enables compact student models to retain much of the performance of cumbersome teachers while meeting practical deployment constraints. When combined with task-aware architecture search, layer-mapping techniques, and online or domain-aware protocols, distillation offers a principled path to build small, fast, and adaptable models across diverse settings.

papers_seen.author: May
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-target (logit) transfer into a broad toolkit that also includes intermediate representation matching, attention- and layer-aware objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combinations with structural compression. Practical deployments of KD require careful choices about which signals to transfer, how to align heterogeneous teacher and student architectures, and how to handle limited or no access to original training data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss in many settings, open problems remain in robustness under distribution shift, privacy- and data-constrained regimes, and principled selection of distilled signals for downstream tasks.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, flexible route to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining a large fraction of teacher performance. KD spans multiple mechanisms — soft-target matching, intermediate-representation transfer, layer-wise or progressive replacement, privacy- and data-aware variants — and can be combined with structural compression such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is highly effective in many realistic settings but is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, what form of knowledge is transferred, data availability (including few-shot or privacy-constrained scenarios), and careful optimization and evaluation. Viewed as a central yet context-sensitive tool, KD should be a default component of compression pipelines, applied in concert with complementary methods and guarded by targeted diagnostics for robustness and rare-token or out-of-distribution behavior.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their accuracy and desirable properties. Methods differ in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure) and in how and when the transfer occurs (offline teacher-to-student, online/co-distillation, adversarial/ensemble-driven, or data-free with synthetic samples). Across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks, KD is routinely combined with architecture-aware choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, and domain-adaptation constraints. Empirical work shows strong gains in efficiency, but also highlights limitations: dependence on teacher quality and data alignment, possible degradation under domain shift or when sensitive attributes are transferred, and open problems in data-free or privacy-preserving settings. This synthesis summarizes key mechanisms, representative variants, cross-modal applications, common engineering practices, and the principal open challenges informed by recent empirical and survey literature.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Trade-offs, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers richer supervisory signals than hard labels—such as softened logits, intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational constraints—and is typically integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and deployment-aware choices (data augmentation, synthetic data, or privacy‑aware aggregation) to meet latency, memory, and device constraints. Its success depends on deliberate design choices about what to transfer, teacher–student capacity alignment, data provenance and availability, and training schedules; common failure modes include degraded rare-token behavior, teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, and privacy or robustness concerns. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable core of compression, combined with monitoring and targeted mitigations for known limits.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger teacher models into smaller, deployable student models so as to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. Over the past decade KD has diversified from matching softened output distributions to a toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schedules, and data-aware protocols (including data-free and synthetic-data approaches). KD is most effective when co-designed with student architectures and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when data and evaluation practices account for domain shift, robustness, and rare-class behaviours. Important open problems remain around principled transfer across heterogeneous architectures, preserving safety-critical or long-tail behavior, data‑free and privacy‑respecting distillation, and understanding what exactly is transferred from teacher to student.
