papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Efficacy, Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and natural language tasks. KD delivers compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while supporting complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and adaptations for data- or privacy-constrained settings. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer (logits, representations, attention maps), how to align teacher and student, and which data strategies and curricula to use. KD should therefore be treated as a first-line, system-level strategy in compression pipelines, but applied with explicit attention to context, complementary techniques, and evaluation of robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Santiago
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression: Position and Practical Recommendations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models because it is methodologically flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and composes naturally with structural compression techniques. KD delivers strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs by transferring soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and can operate with multi‑teacher, online, or data‑synthesis regimes. Its practical value depends on deliberate teacher–student alignment, signal selection, and data strategy, and it must be integrated into broader pipelines that address robustness, fairness, low‑frequency behavior, and privacy. I argue KD is the appropriate default starting point for compression pipelines but must be applied with explicit mitigation and validation steps to avoid known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring useful behavior from large teacher models into smaller student models so the students can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational structure), are implemented in a variety of training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and multi-teacher schedules), and are routinely combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture redesign, and data synthesis). Empirical evidence shows well-designed distillation pipelines often preserve much of a teacher’s performance while delivering substantial gains in efficiency, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data access and provenance, and choices about which signals to transfer. Important open problems include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or domain-specific behaviors (especially in NLP), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and maintaining robustness, fairness, and privacy under compression.

papers_seen.author: Whitney
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applied strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision, language, and multi-modal tasks, distillation methods—ranging from softened-logit matching to intermediate representation, attention, and relational objectives—enable substantial reductions in memory, compute, and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance. Practical deployments integrate KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies) and must manage limitations such as teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, distribution shift, and transfer of undesirable teacher behaviors. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, empirical findings, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from recent literature.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models to smaller student models so that students can be deployed under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. Methods extend beyond matching softened logits to include intermediate representation and attention matching, relational or contrastive objectives, ensemble-to-single schedules, online or co‑distillation, and data‑aware or data‑free variants. In practice, KD is most effective when its signals are chosen to match student capacity and deployment constraints, and when it is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic data). Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or fine‑grained behavior (especially in NLP), aligning heterogeneous architectures, and maintaining robustness, fairness, and privacy under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels — output logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure — and are commonly combined with architecture-level compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and training strategies (online co-training, curriculum schedules, synthetic-data protocols). Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while improving latency and memory usage, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and appropriate choice of transfer signal. Ongoing challenges include robust transfer under distribution shift, aligning heterogeneous architectures, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, and operating in data-limited or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Hart
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models so students can meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy) while retaining much of teacher performance. KD techniques include matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate features or attention maps, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-synthesis or data-free approaches. Success depends on co-designing the distilled signals, student architecture and capacity, and data strategies; complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) are typically applied in concert. Open problems include reliable distillation without original data, robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token or fine-grained behaviors in NLP, and privacy-sensitive protocols.

papers_seen.author: Peters
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring useful information from larger, high-capacity models (teachers) into smaller, faster, or more constrained models (students). Across vision and language tasks, KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's predictive performance. Approaches extend beyond matching final logits to include representation- and attention-level supervision, layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher ensembles, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. Practical deployment combines KD with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and requires attention to data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and task constraints. Open challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, distilling under limited or private data, and ensuring robust transfer of inductive biases and safety properties.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. When designed with task- and capacity-aware choices about what signals to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, relational or attention maps), and when combined with complementary compression primitives and data strategies, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. However, its success is context-dependent: practitioner choices about teacher quality, student architecture, data provenance, selective sample usage, and evaluation under distribution shift determine whether distilled models meet production requirements.

papers_seen.author: Serrano
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A variety of distillation objectives and training regimes have been developed (logit or soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive losses, self-distillation, multi-teacher curricula, and data- or privacy-aware variants). In practice, distillation is most effective when paired with architecture-aware student design, appropriate data strategies (including synthetic or public-data surrogates when original data are unavailable), and complementary compression techniques such as pruning and quantization. Key open challenges remain in reliably transferring rare or long-tail behaviors, preserving robustness and fairness after compression, and designing principled teacher–student curricula across heterogeneous architectures and data regimes.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: Graph-less Neural Networks: Teaching Old MLPs New Tricks via Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are popular for graph machine learning and have shown great results on wide node classification tasks. Yet, they are less popular for practical deployments in the industry owing to their scalability challenges incurred by data dependency. Namely, GNN inference depends on neighbor nodes multiple hops away from the target, and fetching them burdens latency-constrained applications. Existing inference acceleration methods like pruning and quantization can speed up GNNs by reducing Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations, but the improvements are limited given the data dependency is not resolved. Conversely, multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have no graph dependency and infer much faster than GNNs, even though they are less accurate than GNNs for node classification in general. Motivated by these complementary strengths and weaknesses, we bring GNNs and MLPs together via knowledge distillation (KD). Our work shows that the performance of MLPs can be improved by large margins with GNN KD. We call the distilled MLPs Graph-less Neural Networks (GLNNs) as they have no inference graph dependency. We show that GLNNs with competitive accuracy infer faster than GNNs by 146X-273X and faster than other acceleration methods by 14X-27X. Under a production setting involving both transductive and inductive predictions across 7 datasets, GLNN accuracies improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNNs on 6/7 datasets. Comprehensive analysis shows when and why GLNNs can achieve competitive accuracies to GNNs and suggests GLNN as a handy choice for latency-constrained applications.

papers_seen.author: Fisher
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical family of methods for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. Over the past decade KD has evolved from soft-target (logit) matching to a broad toolkit that includes intermediate-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schedules, data-free or synthetic-data approaches, and teacher-free/self-distillation variants. KD is most effective when treated as a system-level design choice—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. While KD routinely yields substantial reductions in inference cost with modest performance loss, its success depends on data availability, optimization dynamics, teacher quality, and careful evaluation of robustness and fairness; open challenges remain around domain shift, preserving rare-token behaviors in language models, privacy-aware distillation, and principled data-free methods.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary Compression Strategy for Practical Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the first-line strategy for compressing large deep models into deployable students: it reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal representations, is broadly applicable across modalities, and composes naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD is not a silver bullet — its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, and how knowledge is represented and aligned — so production pipelines should combine KD with representation-aware objectives, student pretraining, and targeted data strategies to mitigate distributional and optimization pitfalls. When applied with these caveats, KD delivers strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs that make large pretrained models practical for constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Malone
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default Toolkit for Model Compression — Practical, Powerful, but Not Sufficient Alone
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, practical toolkit for compressing deep and language models: it provides flexible supervision channels that routinely yield large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is context dependent and not a standalone cure; its effectiveness hinges on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and explicit checks for robustness and distributional shift. Effective deployment requires composing KD with complementary compression methods, careful co‑design of teacher and student, and evaluation under realistic constraints.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Patterns
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A diverse set of KD mechanisms — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi-teacher or ensemble guidance, self-distillation, and curriculum or task-aware schedules — has been developed and validated across vision, language, and domain-specific tasks. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals to student capacity, leveraging data or synthetic-data strategies when needed, and combining KD with other compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture design). Important open challenges include transferring rare-token or long-tail behavior, preserving robustness and fairness under distribution shift, and automating student design for target resource budgets.

papers_seen.author: Pennington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthetic Review
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used family of techniques for producing compact models from larger teachers so that students retain much of the teachers' predictive power while reducing inference cost and memory footprint. KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a diverse toolkit that includes intermediate-feature imitation, attention and relational matching, multi-teacher and online schedules, self- or teacher-free distillation, and data-free or synthetic-data strategies. Successful distillation requires attention to what knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical results show KD can provide substantial efficiency gains for vision and language tasks, but open challenges remain in robustness to distribution shift, preserving rare or long-tail behaviors, principled data-free methods, and privacy-sensitive settings.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compacts large teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring information beyond hard labels. A spectrum of KD strategies has been developed—soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, many-to-many layer mapping, multi-teacher and progressive schedules, self-distillation, and data-free variants—often combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Empirical work shows well-designed distillation pipelines can recover much of a teacher’s performance while delivering large gains in latency and memory, but outcomes depend on the choice of distillation signal, teacher–student capacity alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints such as domain shift and privacy. Current practical directions emphasize representation-aware objectives, layer-alignment techniques, and hybrid pipelines that treat KD as a core element of system-level compression.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost while preserving predictive performance. KD methods differ in what is transferred (softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals) and in training protocols (offline teacher supervision, online/co-distillation, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants). In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and when practitioner choices account for teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and target-task constraints. While KD routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision and language tasks, its limitations include sensitivity to optimization dynamics, degradation on rare or safety-critical behaviors, and challenges in data-free or privacy-constrained settings. The field offers pragmatic recipes—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning representations, and using data or synthetic surrogates—that produce deployable compact models, but outstanding research questions remain about principled teacher design, robustness under distribution shift, and data-free distillation quality.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central family of techniques for compressing and accelerating deep models by transferring information from larger (teacher) models or training dynamics into smaller (student) models. Across domains and modalities—vision, graph data, speech, and natural language—KD variants address different constraints: limited data or privacy, distributed training, domain shift, and task-specific requirements (e.g., ranking, generation, or sequence modeling). Mechanistically, KD leverages richer supervisory signals than hard labels (soft targets, intermediate features, relational structure, or training trajectories) to regularize students and often yields students that approach teacher accuracy while improving latency and memory. Recent work has clarified connections between KD and other regularizers (e.g., label smoothing), introduced teacher-free and self-distillation approaches, explored the role of data augmentation and feature projectors, and adapted KD to federated, ensemble, and cross-task settings. Empirical results across tasks show KD can enable large compression/acceleration gains with modest performance loss and, in some settings, even improve generalization and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Mitchell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical First-Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as a system-level technique—choosing what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data constraints—KD routinely produces compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical KD pipelines combine diverse signals (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation), and complementary compression steps (progressive module replacement, pruning, quantization) to address domain shifts and deployment constraints. Despite limitations related to teacher–student mismatch and optimization challenges, KD's adaptability across tasks and ability to incorporate robustness and data-free methods make it the recommended primary approach for real-world model compression.

papers_seen.author: Horton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the last decade a diverse toolkit has emerged — soft targets, intermediate representation and attention matching, layer-wise alignments, ensemble and multi-teacher guidance, online/self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants — which practitioners combine with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Empirical results show distillation often preserves much of teacher performance across modalities when objectives and data strategies are matched to student capacity; persistent challenges include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors, avoiding transfer of harmful biases, and building predictive theory about when distillation will succeed.

papers_seen.author: Carroll
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted strategy to compress large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD variants have demonstrated the ability to recover much of a teacher model’s performance while substantially reducing inference latency and memory. Practical deployments treat KD as a flexible, system-level primitive—selecting what to transfer (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), how to expose students to training data (real, synthesized, or online), and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical successes coexist with practical limits: teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors or losing robustness remain active research and engineering concerns.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and compression seek to retain performance of large deep models while reducing size and latency for deployment. Methods extend beyond matching soft teacher outputs to include transferring internal representations, attention maps, and relational or adversarial signals; they can be applied during pretraining, task fine-tuning, or domain adaptation, and may operate with or without access to original training data. Empirical results across retrieval, reading comprehension, pretrained language models, and other domains show consistent trade-offs where careful choice of distillation targets, training curricula, and data augmentation materially improves student generalization and robustness while substantially lowering compute and memory requirements.

papers_seen.author: Burton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First-Line, Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically validated approach for converting large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Treated as a toolkit rather than a single loss, KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), training regimes (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design). I argue KD should serve as the first-line strategy for model compression in modern deep learning and NLP pipelines, provided practitioners adopt principled, context-aware distillation recipes and pair KD with targeted validation for robustness and distributional concerns.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Rationale, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a practical, flexible pathway to compress large deep models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Treated as a system-level toolkit rather than a single loss term, KD supports multiple transfer channels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational signals), composes naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and often yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities. Successful deployment requires careful teacher–student alignment, data or synthetic-data strategies, and explicit checks for robustness, fairness, and rare-token or fine-grained behavior. I argue KD should be the default first‑line strategy for model compression in deep learning and NLP while being applied deliberately and combined with complementary compression primitives and validation under realistic constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Cross-modal Knowledge Distillation for Vision-to-Sensor Action Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Human activity recognition (HAR) based on multi-modal approach has been recently shown to improve the accuracy performance of HAR. However, restricted computational resources associated with wearable devices, i.e., smartwatch, failed to directly support such advanced methods. To tackle this issue, this study introduces an end-to-end Vision-to-Sensor Knowledge Distillation (VSKD) framework. In this VSKD framework, only time-series data, i.e., accelerometer data, is needed from wearable devices during the testing phase. Therefore, this framework will not only reduce the computational demands on edge devices, but also produce a learning model that closely matches the performance of the computational expensive multi-modal approach. In order to retain the local temporal relationship and facilitate visual deep learning models, we first convert time-series data to two-dimensional images by applying the Gramian Angular Field ( GAF) based encoding method. We adopted ResNet18 and multi-scale TRN with BN-Inception as teacher and student network in this study, respectively. A novel loss function, named Distance and Angle-wised Semantic Knowledge loss (DASK), is proposed to mitigate the modality variations between the vision and the sensor domain. Extensive experimental results on UTD-MHAD, MMAct, and Berkeley-MHAD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and competitiveness of the proposed VSKD model which can deployed on wearable sensors.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Findings, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring useful predictive behavior or internal structure from one or more teachers. A rich set of KD approaches exists — from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate representation imitation, attention and feature alignment, adversarial and projector-based techniques, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free or federated variants — and these have been applied across NLP, vision, graph-structured data, multimodal models, and generative models. Empirical work shows KD often recovers much of teacher performance while reducing inference cost, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher/student compatibility, data availability, and task-specific constraints. Important practical concerns include preserving rare-token behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher errors or biases, enabling privacy-preserving or data-free compression, and combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search).

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Failure Modes, and Practical Recipes
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central tool for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across vision, speech, recommendation, and NLP. KD techniques range from simple logits matching to representation-level transfer, multi-teacher schemes, adversarial sample synthesis, and progressive module replacement. While many distillation recipes recover most of a teacher’s accuracy and enable large efficiency gains, the success of KD depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student capacities, and how to handle limited or absent training data. Careful design—matching distillation targets to student capacity, mitigating transferred errors, and combining distillation with complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search)—yields robust, efficient models for practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Improving the Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks with Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep Neural Networks have achieved huge success at a wide spectrum of applications from language modeling, computer vision to speech recognition. However, nowadays, good performance alone is not sufficient to satisfy the needs of practical deployment where interpretability is demanded for cases involving ethics and mission critical applications. The complex models of Deep Neural Networks make it hard to understand and reason the predictions, which hinders its further progress. To tackle this problem, we apply the Knowledge Distillation technique to distill Deep Neural Networks into decision trees in order to attain good performance and interpretability simultaneously. We formulate the problem at hand as a multi-output regression problem and the experiments demonstrate that the student model achieves significantly better accuracy performance (about 1\% to 5\%) than vanilla decision trees at the same level of tree depth. The experiments are implemented on the TensorFlow platform to make it scalable to big datasets. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to distill Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets.

papers_seen.author: Barker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line but Contextual Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD provides multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals) and training regimes (offline teacher-to-student, online/self-distillation, ensemble-to-single), and it can be combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. However, KD’s success depends on careful teacher–student co-design, the choice of what knowledge to transfer, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness and privacy. Treated as a core element of a compression pipeline rather than a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy, KD yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs for many real-world applications while leaving important open problems in data-free distillation, rare-behavior preservation, and distributional robustness.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Backbone of Model Compression: Capabilities, Variants, and Contextual Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact, deployable models from large teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD supports a broad set of objectives—matching logits, aligning internal representations, using online or multi-teacher schemes, and operating with or without original training data—so it serves as the backbone of many modern compression pipelines. However, its success is context-dependent: choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability, and deployment constraints determine outcomes, and KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques and principled training workflows.

papers_seen.author: Alexander
papers_seen.title: Make Knowledge Distillation the Core of Compression Pipelines — With Careful Complementary Design
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first-line strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. KD offers a flexible toolkit that can transfer soft outputs, intermediate representations, and relational signals, and it integrates naturally with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, data-free synthesis). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success requires deliberate choices about which signals to transfer, alignment of teacher and student capacity and architecture, data availability and provenance, and safeguards for robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy. Combining KD with targeted complementary methods and data-aware practices yields the best practical accuracy–efficiency trade-offs for deep learning and NLP systems.

papers_seen.author: Thomas
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a multifaceted and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. A broad family of distillation signals and training regimes—ranging from softened logits to intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational or contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules, adversarial and data-free methods, and task-aware curricula—enables substantial reductions in parameter counts, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on co-designing distillation targets with student architectures, combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), and addressing data, robustness, fairness, and privacy concerns. Remaining challenges include reliably transferring rare or long-tail behaviors, coping with distribution shift and limited or private data, and forming principled teacher–student curricula across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Pitts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, practitioners use softened output distributions, intermediate-feature matching, attention- or relation-level signals, multi-teacher and online schedules, and self-distillation. Distillation is typically combined with complementary compression (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and with data strategies that range from using distilled teacher outputs to synthetic or data-free approaches. Empirical successes include large reductions in inference cost while preserving most of the teacher’s performance, but failures arise when teacher–student misalignment, data mismatch, low-frequency outputs, or privacy constraints are not addressed. Practical pipelines treat distillation as a flexible, context-aware toolkit rather than a fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default Compression Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP: Rationale and Practical Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the default, first‑line strategy for compressing large neural models in deep learning and NLP because it provides flexible, task‑aware transfer channels that preserve predictive behavior while enabling complementary structural compression. KD excels when combined with architecture-aware design, representation-level alignment, and data strategies that address limited or private training data. A practical KD-first pipeline—selecting appropriate transfer signals, applying task-aware layer mappings, leveraging data-free or augmentation methods when needed, and composing KD with pruning/quantization—yields robust, high-compression students suitable for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. The literature frames KD as a multifaceted toolkit—ranging from logit-level soft-target matching to representation- and attention-level alignment, multi-teacher schedules, data-free and privacy-aware procedures, and compositions with structural compression such as pruning and quantization. Empirical work shows KD often preserves much of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in memory and latency, but success depends on teacher–student compatibility, availability and quality of data, and careful selection of distillation signals and optimization protocols. Practical pipelines therefore combine multiple KD strategies with complementary compression techniques and task-aware adaptations to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wolfe
papers_seen.title: Robust and Resource-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation by Generative Pseudo Replay
papers_seen.abstract: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD) allows knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a more compact one (student) in the absence of original training data. Existing works use a validation set to monitor the accuracy of the student over real data and report the highest performance throughout the entire process. However, validation data may not be available at distillation time either, making it infeasible to record the student snapshot that achieved the peak accuracy. Therefore, a practical data-free KD method should be robust and ideally provide monotonically increasing student accuracy during distillation. This is challenging because the student experiences knowledge degradation due to the distribution shift of the synthetic data. A straightforward approach to overcome this issue is to store and rehearse the generated samples periodically, which increases the memory footprint and creates privacy concerns. We propose to model the distribution of the previously observed synthetic samples with a generative network. In particular, we design a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) with a training objective that is customized to learn the synthetic data representations optimally. The student is rehearsed by the generative pseudo replay technique, with samples produced by the VAE. Hence knowledge degradation can be prevented without storing any samples. Experiments on image classification benchmarks show that our method optimizes the expected value of the distilled model accuracy while eliminating the large memory overhead incurred by the sample-storing methods.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression approaches transfer information from larger, high-capacity models to smaller, deployable students or otherwise reduce model complexity while preserving task performance. Across vision and NLP, practitioners use a range of supervision signals and training protocols—soft-target matching, feature and attention imitation, representation-level objectives, self-distillation, online co-training, and data-free generation—to trade off accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation signals and training recipes can produce compact models that approach teacher performance, but success depends on student capacity, data availability, and alignment between teacher signals and downstream tasks. Open challenges include robust transfer of rare-token behavior, principled selection of what to distill, and scaling distillation to privacy-sensitive or distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, efficient students for deployment in deep learning and NLP. A broad family of KD techniques—ranging from softened-logit supervision to intermediate representation matching, attention- and feature-level imitation, many-to-many layer alignment, adversarial and data-free variants, and task- or device-aware architecture search—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while often retaining most of the teacher's performance. Effective application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, whether and how to use original data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. Important open problems remain regarding theoretical understanding, robustness under distribution shift or imperfect teachers, and scalable private or data-free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD variants transfer information via softened outputs, intermediate representations, attention or relational signals, and adversarially or synthetically generated inputs. When combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, or data strategies, KD supports deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, success depends on careful matching of what is transferred to student capacity, handling data scarcity or distribution shift, and mitigating propagation of teacher errors. This synthesis summarizes common mechanisms, representative algorithmic families, empirical patterns, and actionable recommendations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Zavala
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, efficient students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A broad family of KD techniques has been developed—matching softened logits, aligning intermediate representations or attention, using multi-teacher or online co-training schedules, and synthesizing or augmenting data for training students. KD often recovers much of a teacher's performance while reducing parameter count and inference cost, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data alignment, and training dynamics. Practical deployments combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, progressive module replacement) and must address open challenges including heterogeneous or federated settings, data scarcity or privacy constraints, robustness under distribution shift, and preservation of low-frequency or domain-specific signals.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Context‑Dependent Core Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD operates through multiple mechanisms — softened-output transfer, intermediate-representation matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and synthetic-data strategies — and is most effective when treated as a system-level design choice that aligns teacher signals, student capacity, and available data. While KD routinely delivers strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs, its reliability depends on careful co-design, complementary compression methods, and explicit handling of domain shift, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students in deep learning and NLP. When designed with task- and capacity-aware choices about what signals to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, relational or attention maps), and when combined with complementary compression primitives and data strategies, KD routinely produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing inference cost. However, its success is context-dependent: practitioner choices about teacher quality, student architecture, data provenance, selective sample usage, and evaluation under distribution shift determine whether distilled models meet production requirements.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Strengths, Mechanisms, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller students that are deployable under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. When applied thoughtfully—choosing what to transfer (logits, intermediate representations, relational signals), aligning teacher and student architectures and tokenization, and combining KD with complementary techniques such as architecture search or targeted pruning—distillation routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance and sometimes even improve generalization. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on data availability, teacher quality and friendliness, domain shifts, and the specific form of knowledge chosen for transfer. Effective deployment therefore requires principled design of the distillation objective, curricula or annealing schedules, and safeguards for robustness and rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a pragmatic, widely applicable tool for shrinking large deep models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment. When combined with complementary practices — careful teacher selection or adaptation, pre-training of compact architectures, feature-level matching, and privacy- or data-aware workflows — KD yields most of the practical benefits of compression while exposing clear trade-offs and failure modes. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the backbone of model compression pipelines, but that realizing reliable production gains requires principled choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Ramsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, System‑Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an adaptable, empirically grounded approach for transferring the behavior of large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a system-level primitive rather than a single loss, KD can provide multiple types of supervisory signals, interface with complementary compression methods, and be shaped by data- and deployment-aware choices. Adopting KD as a first‑line strategy enables strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs in many realistic settings, provided practitioners explicitly address teacher–student compatibility, data provenance, and known risks such as distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Transferring Inductive Biases through Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Having the right inductive biases can be crucial in many tasks or scenarios where data or computing resources are a limiting factor, or where training data is not perfectly representative of the conditions at test time. However, defining, designing and efficiently adapting inductive biases is not necessarily straightforward. In this paper, we explore the power of knowledge distillation for transferring the effect of inductive biases from one model to another. We consider families of models with different inductive biases, LSTMs vs. Transformers and CNNs vs. MLPs, in the context of tasks and scenarios where having the right inductive biases is critical. We study the effect of inductive biases on the solutions the models converge to and investigate how and to what extent the effect of inductive biases is transferred through knowledge distillation, in terms of not only performance but also different aspects of converged solutions.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques compress large, high-performance models into smaller, faster models by transferring knowledge from a teacher to a student. Recent work spans many complementary strategies — logit/soft-target matching, feature and layer-wise distillation, structural and channel-level transformations, data-free generation of proxy inputs, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and task-aware filtering — and addresses practical concerns such as cross-domain transfer, limited compute, and maintaining task performance in NLP settings. Progress includes specialized algorithms for pre-trained language model compression, algorithmic and architectural enhancements that reduce capacity gaps, and theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Together these developments offer a toolkit for deploying compact models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive environments while preserving most of the original model performance.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as the System‑Level Core of Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood and used as a system‑level, context‑aware toolkit for compressing large models into deployable students. KD reliably provides large gains in latency, memory, and energy efficiency by transferring soft targets, intermediate representations, and relational signals, and it composes naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. However, KD is not a universal panacea: its benefits depend on teacher–student alignment, the nature and availability of distillation data, and careful handling of robustness, fairness, and privacy concerns. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a first‑line strategy within a broader compression pipeline that integrates complementary methods, targeted data techniques, and explicit evaluation for out‑of‑distribution or rare behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. KD encompasses multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational structure) and can be adapted to settings with limited or no access to original training data, heterogeneous or federated deployments, and domain-specific constraints. Best outcomes arise when distillation is combined with task-aware student design, appropriate distillation targets, and data or augmentation strategies matched to deployment needs.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Theory, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. The field comprises a family of methods that transfer different forms of information—from soft logits to internal representations, attention maps, and relational structure—and integrates naturally with complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Success depends on choosing what to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacities and architectures, managing data availability (including data-free or federated setups), and designing appropriate optimization curricula. While KD routinely yields favorable trade-offs between efficiency and accuracy across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, important limitations remain around teacher–student mismatch, domain shift, rare-token preservation in NLP, and robustness under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often over-parameterized teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD strategies vary in what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate representations, relations), how it is transferred (logit matching, feature-mimicking, projector layers, contrastive objectives, adversarial losses), and in deployment settings (data-available, data-free, federated or distributed, and online). Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance while enabling practical gains in speed and memory; however, method choice, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and distributional shifts materially affect outcomes, and open problems remain in preserving rare-token behavior, transferring robustness and fairness, and compressing across heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Primary but Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the first-line strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students because it consistently yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when thoughtfully applied. Its practical success depends on careful selection of what to transfer (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals), co-design of teacher and student architectures, appropriate data and augmentation strategies, and combination with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD is not a universal cure: capacity mismatch, limited or private data, distribution shift, and preservation of rare or safety‑critical behaviors require explicit mitigation and evaluation. A pragmatic pipeline treats KD as the core compression primitive while integrating targeted remedies for its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Ray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Representation-aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a toolbox—combining soft-target supervision, intermediate representation matching, attention- or layer-aware mappings, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-conscious strategies—KD yields compact models that better preserve teacher behavior while meeting deployment constraints. However, realizing those benefits requires attention to teacher–student compatibility, choice of distilled signals, and data constraints; KD is powerful but not a universal remedy.

papers_seen.author: Zimmerman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practice, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels. A broad and growing set of techniques—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, multi-teacher and ensemble schedules, data-free synthesis, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations—enables compact models to approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and deployment constraints. Effective application depends on careful teacher–student design, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods; open issues remain around robustness, rare-token behavior, privacy, and heterogeneous architecture alignment.
