papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. Across NLP, speech, vision, and recommendation systems, KD reduces inference cost and memory, enables deployment on constrained devices, and can transfer specialized capabilities when paired with appropriate data and training choices. Its effectiveness depends on what is distilled (soft targets, intermediate features, relational signals), the availability and synthesis of training data, and teacher–student design; complementary compression tools and safeguards addressing bias, privacy, and distributional mismatch are often required for robust, real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Practical Principles for Effective Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression are indispensable tools to deploy high-performing deep models under compute, memory, privacy, and latency constraints. Across modalities and tasks, effective compression requires more than copying teacher logits: practitioners should match richer internal representations, align inputs and tokenization across teacher and student, design teacher updates that explicitly optimize transfer, and account for privacy and robustness needs. When applied thoughtfully, KD can produce compact models that retain much of the teacher’s utility and in some cases improve efficiency beyond the original models.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Distilling the Knowledge of BERT for Sequence-to-Sequence ASR
papers_seen.abstract: Attention-based sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models have achieved promising results in automatic speech recognition (ASR). However, as these models decode in a left-to-right way, they do not have access to context on the right. We leverage both left and right context by applying BERT as an external language model to seq2seq ASR through knowledge distillation. In our proposed method, BERT generates soft labels to guide the training of seq2seq ASR. Furthermore, we leverage context beyond the current utterance as input to BERT. Experimental evaluations show that our method significantly improves the ASR performance from the seq2seq baseline on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ). Knowledge distillation from BERT outperforms that from a transformer LM that only looks at left context. We also show the effectiveness of leveraging context beyond the current utterance. Our method outperforms other LM application approaches such as n-best rescoring and shallow fusion, while it does not require extra inference cost.

papers_seen.author: Lynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Trade‑offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfers information from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Across vision, speech, and NLP, KD has evolved from soft‑logit matching to richer objectives that align intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational structure; it is routinely combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (data‑free synthesis, selective sampling). Empirical practice shows KD delivers strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when teacher quality, student capacity, distillation signals, and data are co‑designed for deployment, but important limitations remain around robustness, long‑tail/rare behaviour, privacy, and reliable distillation without original data.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from teacher(s) to student(s). Advances span logit- and feature-based matching, multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, data-free and federated scenarios, and domain- or task-specific adaptations in NLP. Practical work shows KD can yield large reductions in model size and inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance, but design choices (what to match, how to weight teachers, whether data are available, and deployment constraints) strongly affect outcomes. Remaining challenges include robustness to domain shift, privacy and communication constraints in distributed settings, and principled handling of teacher–student mismatches.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods that transfers richer supervision from large teacher models to compact students in order to reduce inference cost while retaining predictive performance. KD covers logit/soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, channel- and feature-level transfers, self- and online-distillation, and multi-teacher and data-free variants. Its effectiveness depends on alignment between teacher and student capacity, the choice of what to transfer, data availability, and deployment constraints; therefore KD should be treated as a central component of modern compression pipelines but always applied with task- and context-aware adaptations and complementary compression primitives.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has evolved from matching softened logits to a broad family of methods that include intermediate-feature alignment, attention- and relation-based transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schedules, data-free or synthetic-data strategies, and architecture-aware compression. Practically, KD enables favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks but requires careful design around the form of knowledge transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability and augmentation, and evaluation for robustness and undesired behavior. Open problems remain in reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare or low-frequency behaviors in sequence tasks, and ensuring fairness and robustness in deployed compact models.

papers_seen.author: Novak
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of methods for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models so that the students retain much of the teachers' performance while meeting resource, latency, or privacy constraints. KD methods include matching teacher output distributions, aligning intermediate representations or attention, synthesizing surrogate training data when original data are unavailable, and deploying progressive or ensemble-based strategies. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or search) and training-time strategies (curricula, online distillation, or federated protocols) to balance efficiency and accuracy. Despite strong empirical success across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in aligning heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, operating under limited or private data, and designing principled objectives and curricula that preserve robustness and task-specific inductive biases.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Variants, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a central strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher’s predictive power. A variety of mechanisms—soft-target matching, intermediate feature imitation, layer- or module-level mappings, and architecture-aware search—enable trade-offs among accuracy, latency, model size, and privacy. Practical deployments combine distillation with complementary methods (pretraining of compact architectures, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, and privacy-preserving synthesis) and tailor choices to data availability, task constraints, and target hardware. Despite broad empirical success, open issues remain around transferring robustness and rare-token behavior, aligning heterogeneous architectures, and designing distillation pipelines that are robust under limited or private data.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical, multi-strategy approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD transfers richer supervisory signals than hard labels — soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational constraints, or ensemble targets — and composes naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware redesign). Empirically, distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success depends on careful choices about what knowledge to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability (including data-free or privacy-sensitive regimes), and training protocols; important open problems remain in robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token or safety-critical behaviors, and principled design of distillation objectives.

papers_seen.author: Peterson
papers_seen.title: Understanding Knowledge Distillation in Non-autoregressive Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems predict a sequence of output tokens in parallel, achieving substantial improvements in generation speed compared to autoregressive models. Existing NAT models usually rely on the technique of knowledge distillation, which creates the training data from a pretrained autoregressive model for better performance. Knowledge distillation is empirically useful, leading to large gains in accuracy for NAT models, but the reason for this success has, as of yet, been unclear. In this paper, we first design systematic experiments to investigate why knowledge distillation is crucial to NAT training. We find that knowledge distillation can reduce the complexity of data sets and help NAT to model the variations in the output data. Furthermore, a strong correlation is observed between the capacity of an NAT model and the optimal complexity of the distilled data for the best translation quality. Based on these findings, we further propose several approaches that can alter the complexity of data sets to improve the performance of NAT models. We achieve the state-of-the-art performance for the NAT-based models, and close the gap with the autoregressive baseline on WMT14 En-De benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. KD encompasses soft-target matching, intermediate-representation alignment, relational or contrastive objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, and data-aware variants (including data-free and federated protocols). Empirical evidence shows KD frequently yields strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs across vision, NLP, speech, graph, and multi-task settings, but success depends on student capacity, teacher–student alignment, available data (or generators), and attention to robustness, privacy, and long-tail phenomena. Practical pipelines treat KD as one component of compression that should be combined with architecture-aware design, pruning, quantization, and careful training curricula.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has expanded from simple soft-target matching to a diverse toolkit—intermediate representation and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-teaching schedules, and data-aware or data-free variants—and is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical application requires careful teacher–student co‑design, data strategies appropriate to deployment constraints, and targeted mitigations for known failure modes such as distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and inadvertent transfer of undesirable behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core First-Line Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP — Powerful, Context‑Dependent, and Best Used in Integrated Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile method for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When done beyond naïve soft-label copying—e.g., via intermediate-representation matching, attention or layer alignment, and careful teacher–student design—KD routinely delivers large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. Its strongest role is as a first-line, representation-aware strategy that is combined with complementary compression techniques and data strategies. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, data availability, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors and distributional failures. Practical deployment therefore requires principled recipes, diagnostics for failure modes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Ramsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default, System‑Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an adaptable, empirically grounded approach for transferring the behavior of large teacher models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a system-level primitive rather than a single loss, KD can provide multiple types of supervisory signals, interface with complementary compression methods, and be shaped by data- and deployment-aware choices. Adopting KD as a first‑line strategy enables strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs in many realistic settings, provided practitioners explicitly address teacher–student compatibility, data provenance, and known risks such as distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Mechanisms, Practices, and Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large teacher models into smaller students by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels alone. A broad family of distillation methods—matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention, self-distillation, and ensemble-to-single-model compression—has been applied across vision and language tasks to reduce inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on what is distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, what data are available or synthesized for transfer, and how distillation is integrated with complementary compression techniques. Key open problems include principled selection of distilled signals for a target student and task, robustness and fairness under compression, handling limited or private data, and optimizing teacher–student compatibility.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First‑Line, Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible approach for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. Across vision, language, and graph settings, KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation alignment, attention and relational knowledge transfer, multi-teacher schedules, and data‑aware or data‑free variants. When KD is applied as part of an integrated compression pipeline—together with architecture-aware student design, pruning, quantization, and data strategies—it routinely yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, teacher–student capacity alignment, the choice of distilled signals, the provenance and amount of data, and robustness/privacy requirements. Best practice treats KD as a first‑line mechanism that must be configured and evaluated for the target deployment context rather than used naively.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, System-Level Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a system-level design paradigm—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining distillation with complementary compression steps—KD routinely yields strong efficiency–accuracy trade-offs. However, its success is context-dependent: careful attention to teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and robustness or privacy constraints is required for reliable deployment.

papers_seen.author: Harmon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural teachers into smaller student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Across vision and language tasks, KD techniques include soft-target matching, intermediate-feature imitation, attention- or relation-based alignment, self-distillation, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or domain-aware variations. Empirical work shows that distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design to meet deployment constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, available data, and training objectives. Remaining challenges include reliable distillation without original data, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, transferring robustness and inductive biases, and handling heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive environments.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for turning large, high-performing neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. As a toolkit, KD spans soft-target (logit) transfer, intermediate representation matching, layer- or module-level mapping, progressive replacement strategies, and online or multi-teacher regimes. KD yields large gains in memory, latency, and energy efficiency while often retaining most of teacher performance, but its success is conditional on teacher–student alignment, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation strategies, and attention to robustness and privacy. Practitioners should treat KD as a central element of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with architecture-aware design, pruning/quantization, and careful evaluation—rather than a one-size-fits-all remedy.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Boyd
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Research over the past decade has produced a diverse set of objectives and training regimes—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and layer-wise alignment, attention/relational signals, data- or privacy-aware synthesis, and teacher–student co-design—that together enable substantial reductions in inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, available data, teacher/student compatibility, and complementary compression techniques; open challenges include robust transfer under domain shift, distillation without original data, and principled handling of heterogeneous or privacy-sensitive deployments.

papers_seen.author: Vasquez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core but Insufficient Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably yields favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs across modalities when its signals, data, and student architectures are co-designed with deployment constraints. However, real-world compression requires integrating KD with complementary methods and system-level choices to handle teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, robustness, and task-specific complexities.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically supported approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. When thoughtfully applied — selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student architectures, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques and data strategies — distillation enables large reductions in compute and memory with modest performance loss. However, KD is not universally sufficient on its own: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and provenance, and optimization choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat distillation as a core element of a broader compression strategy, integrating pretraining, representation-aware objectives, multi-teacher curricula, and privacy- or data-constrained methods to produce robust, efficient models for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, retrieval, and generation tasks. Contemporary KD methods extend far beyond simple soft-label matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational objectives, curriculum and online schemes, multi-teacher and data-free variants, and tight integrations with architecture-level compression such as pruning and quantization. Empirical work shows KD can preserve much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on matched teacher–student design, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthetic-data alternatives, and careful evaluation of robustness, fairness, and rare-class behaviors. Open challenges remain in domain-shift robustness, privacy-sensitive distillation, automated student architecture design, and principled selection of which aspects of teacher knowledge to transfer.

papers_seen.author: Medina
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a flexible, practical toolkit for compressing large neural networks into smaller, deployable models. Methods extend beyond simple soft-target (logit) matching to include alignment of intermediate representations, attention maps, relational structure, and architecture-aware adaptations. In practice KD is combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data‑free approaches), and training curricula (annealing, multi-teacher or online schedules). Empirical work across vision and language shows that carefully designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and design choices that affect robustness, fairness, and generalization under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Carter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression: Effectiveness, Limits, and Practical Pipeline
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. When treated as a system—choosing which signals to transfer (logits, features, attention), aligning teacher and student architectures, managing data and sample selection, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques—KD yields strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP tasks. Its practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and attention to robustness and rare-token behavior; hence KD is best used as the central element of a broader compression pipeline rather than as a standalone fix.

papers_seen.author: Ruiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for transferring knowledge from large teacher models to smaller student models so the students meet deployment constraints (latency, memory, compute, and privacy) while retaining much of teacher performance. KD encompasses matching softened outputs, aligning intermediate representations or attention maps, using multi- or online-teacher schedules, and employing data-aware or data-free synthesis; it is frequently combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful student design. Empirical practice emphasizes co-design of distillation signals, student capacity and architecture, and data or augmentation strategies, while ongoing challenges include reliable distillation without original data, robust transfer under domain shift, preservation of rare or fine-grained behaviors in NLP, and privacy and fairness considerations.

papers_seen.author: Fowler

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable approach for compressing modern deep models across modalities. When combined with architecture-aware transformations, feature-level supervision, multi-teacher signals, and careful handling of data constraints, KD enables compact students that retain most of a teacher's effectiveness while meeting latency, memory, and domain requirements. However, distillation artifacts and data limitations require methodic choices—e.g., feature mimicking, confidence-aware multi-teacher weighting, or generative replay—to avoid propagating teacher errors or overfitting in low-data regimes.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: A Balanced Position
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the central, practical backbone of model-compression pipelines in deep learning and NLP: it offers a flexible toolkit to transfer predictive behavior and internal structure from large teachers to compact students, enabling large efficiency gains while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal remedy — its success depends on careful selection of distillation signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies (including data-free or synthetic-data methods), and complementary compression steps; production-grade deployment therefore requires disciplined evaluation of robustness, fairness, and task-specific behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Bender
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical Core for Model Compression: Capabilities, Limits, and Recommended Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded toolkit that enables compressing large deep and language models into smaller, deployable students. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels—ranging from softened outputs to intermediate representations and relational signals—KD routinely yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs when paired with architecture-aware design and complementary compression methods. However, its effectiveness is context-dependent: success requires matching distilled signals to student capacity, careful teacher–student co-design, data strategies (including synthetic or data-free approaches), and explicit attention to robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy concerns. Treating KD as the backbone of an integrated compression pipeline delivers the best practical outcomes while acknowledging and mitigating its failure modes.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal signals so students meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. The field has evolved from soft-label matching to a rich toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention alignment, multi- and online-teacher schedules, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis; KD is frequently combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-aware pretraining. Empirical and emerging theoretical work highlight both KD’s practical utility and its limits — success depends on teacher–student compatibility, availability and provenance of data, choice of transferred signals, and optimization curricula — motivating integrated pipelines and ongoing research on robustness, rare-token fidelity in sequence tasks, and privacy-preserving distillation.

papers_seen.title: BERT-EMD: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression with Earth Mover's Distance
papers_seen.abstract: Pre-trained language models (e.g., BERT) have achieved significant success in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. However, high storage and computational costs obstruct pre-trained language models to be effectively deployed on resource-constrained devices. In this paper, we propose a novel BERT distillation method based on many-to-many layer mapping, which allows each intermediate student layer to learn from any intermediate teacher layers. In this way, our model can learn from different teacher layers adaptively for various NLP tasks. %motivated by the intuition that different NLP tasks require different levels of linguistic knowledge contained in the intermediate layers of BERT. In addition, we leverage Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) to compute the minimum cumulative cost that must be paid to transform knowledge from teacher network to student network. EMD enables the effective matching for many-to-many layer mapping. %EMD can be applied to network layers with different sizes and effectively measures semantic distance between the teacher network and student network. Furthermore, we propose a cost attention mechanism to learn the layer weights used in EMD automatically, which is supposed to further improve the model's performance and accelerate convergence time. Extensive experiments on GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our model achieves competitive performance compared to strong competitors in terms of both accuracy and model compression.

papers_seen.author: Martin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and pragmatic approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD can transfer predictive behavior and internal representations, and—when co-designed with architecture choices, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques—routinely yields compact models that meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability and provenance, token- or class-level coverage in the teacher, and careful handling of optimization dynamics and robustness. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, system-level tool for model compression in deep learning and NLP, used together with targeted engineering and auditing to manage its limits and to maximize practical benefit.

When co‑designed with student architectures, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, module replacement), distillation routinely yields substantial reductions in latency, memory, and energy while preserving much of teacher performance. Practical compression usually pairs distillation with architecture-aware strategies (pruning, quantization, or search) and careful design choices about what, how, and when to transfer knowledge; success depends on teacher quality, data availability, teacher–student compatibility, and attention to robustness and privacy.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring richer supervisory signals than hard labels. Over the past decade KD has diversified into a toolkit that includes logits and softened-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, many-to-many layer alignment, multi-teacher and online schedules, and data-side interventions (including data-free synthesis). When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student co-design, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while delivering substantial gains in latency and memory. Effectiveness depends on the choice of distillation signal, teacher and student capacity alignment, the availability and provenance of distillation data, and deployment constraints such as domain shift, privacy, and robustness. Practical pipelines treat KD as a system-level primitive that must be adapted to task and context rather than a one-size-fits-all procedure.

papers_seen.author: Kidd
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. Practitioners apply KD not only as a logits-matching loss but as a system-level design primitive that includes representation matching, multi-teacher fusion, data and curriculum design, and combination with pruning and quantization. Its empirical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer (soft labels, intermediate features, relational signals), how to map teacher signals to potentially heterogeneous students, and how to handle limited or private data. While KD often yields compact models with near-teacher performance and useful regularization effects, limitations remain: imperfect teacher signals, optimization challenges, robustness and fairness transfer, and domain-shift or data-scarce scenarios. Current best practices emphasize task-aware selection of distilled signals, layer/projector alignment, and hybrid pipelines that combine KD with other compression techniques to meet deployment constraints.

Treating KD as the first-line tool within an integrated compression pipeline—rather than a one-size-fits-all loss—delivers the most reliable outcomes while pointing to open research on robustness, data-free distillation, and privacy-preserving protocols.

papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from teacher to student. A diverse set of approaches extend the basic soft-label paradigm to include internal representation matching, layer-wise and attention-guided alignment, task-aware selection of distilled features, data-free or zero-shot synthesis of training examples, augmentation-driven consistency, multi-teacher and ensemble transfer, adversarial learning objectives, and architecture search tailored to downstream tasks. These techniques improve inference efficiency while aiming to preserve accuracy, generalization, and task-specific behavior; they also enable distillation in settings with limited or no access to original training data and in generation tasks. Ongoing challenges include aligning heterogeneous architectures, selecting which teacher knowledge to preserve for a given student capacity and task, and designing robust distilled models that generalize across domains and data shifts.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Valencia
papers_seen.title: Beyond Soft Labels: Toward Representation- and Strategy-driven Knowledge Distillation for Efficient and Robust NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation remains a central approach to compress large deep learning models for deployment in resource-constrained and domain-specific NLP settings. I argue that to realize reliably compact and generalizable student models we must move past sole reliance on teacher soft-labels and adopt representation-aware objectives, structured channel/feature matching, adaptive training curricula, and practical strategies for low-precision, data-limited, and privacy-sensitive scenarios. Combining these approaches yields students that better capture teacher knowledge, adapt to new domains, and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Mann
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. A wide family of KD methods—soft logits, intermediate representation matching, attention- and relation-based losses, multi-teacher and online schemes, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and teacher- or student-aware curricula—enables substantial reductions in model size and latency across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Practical success depends on coherent system design: choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student capacity and architectures, selecting or synthesizing appropriate data, and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). While KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can sometimes improve generalization, it has limits related to teacher–student mismatch, distributional shift, rare-token preservation in NLP, and privacy/robustness tradeoffs. Best practice treats KD as one component of a broader, task- and deployment-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Andrews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD spans logit-level supervision, representation- and attention-level imitation, multi-teacher and online schemes, and specialized adaptations for data-limited or privacy-sensitive settings. When combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and careful teacher–student co‑design, KD routinely produces compact models that preserve much of teacher performance. Nonetheless, success depends on signal choice, capacity alignment, data provenance, and attention to robustness, fairness, and distribution shift; several open technical and evaluation questions remain for production deployment.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining predictive performance. Over the past decade KD has expanded beyond softened-logit matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schedules, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. When combined with complementary compression methods and careful teacher–student co-design, KD forms a practical backbone for producing deployable models, although important open problems remain around robustness, domain shift, privacy, and preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible strategy for compressing large models into smaller, faster students suitable for deployment in constrained environments. Advances across task-adaptive compression, data-free and zero-shot distillation, multi-teacher and meta-learned teaching, and self-distillation demonstrate KD's broad applicability. However, KD is not a panacea: success depends on data availability, the teacher–student optimization dynamics, and explicit design choices around architecture and training signals. Combining pre-training of compact models, task-aware architecture search, and sophisticated distillation protocols yields the best trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, pragmatic family of methods for producing compact models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. Empirical work shows KD can transfer rich supervisory signals beyond hard labels—ranging from softened logits to internal representations, attention patterns, and relational objectives—and that carefully designed distillation pipelines often recover most of a teacher’s performance while greatly reducing inference cost. In practice KD is most effective when co-designed with student architectures and combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and targeted data strategies; its limits include sensitivity to teacher–student mismatch, reliance on appropriate distillation data, potential transfer of undesirable behaviors, and challenges around robustness, rare-case behavior, and privacy. These strengths and limits motivate treating KD as a core element of compression workflows rather than a universal, standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) effectively compresses large, high-performing models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or ensemble consensus. KD has matured into a versatile toolkit that, when combined with careful teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), yields compact models that approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and targeted objectives. Best practice therefore treats distillation as the central element of a compression pipeline, augmented by augmentation, curriculum design, privacy-aware aggregation, and architecture-aware substitution to mitigate known failure modes and preserve robustness and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Flynn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and selected internal information from teacher models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and training regimes—soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature or attention alignment, multi-teacher and ensemble supervision, adversarial or data-free variants, and task- or device-aware architecture search—enable substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving much of teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals to student capacity, choosing appropriate data and augmentation, and combining KD with complementary compression techniques; open problems remain in theoretical explanation, cross-distribution robustness, and preserving rare-token or fairness-sensitive behavior.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Multi-Level Branched Regularization for Federated Learning
papers_seen.abstract: A critical challenge of federated learning is data heterogeneity and imbalance across clients, which leads to inconsistency between local networks and unstable convergence of global models. To alleviate the limitations, we propose a novel architectural regularization technique that constructs multiple auxiliary branches in each local model by grafting local and global subnetworks at several different levels and that learns the representations of the main pathway in the local model congruent to the auxiliary hybrid pathways via online knowledge distillation. The proposed technique is effective to robustify the global model even in the non-iid setting and is applicable to various federated learning frameworks conveniently without incurring extra communication costs. We perform comprehensive empirical studies and demonstrate remarkable performance gains in terms of accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods. The source code is available at our project page.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Mahoney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and empirically effective approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. By transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone—ranging from softened logits to intermediate features, attention maps, and multi-teacher signals—KD enables compact models that preserve much of teacher performance while supporting complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture-aware transforms). KD also enables specialized workflows when data are limited or private (e.g., data-free distillation) and can be adapted to preserve robustness or domain-specific expertise. Realizing KD’s full potential requires careful choices about the form of knowledge, teacher–student alignment, and training curricula, but when these are handled methodically KD provides a practical, general toolkit for deploying high-quality compact models in resource-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When applied with attention to what knowledge is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention or relational signals), how teachers and students are aligned, and how data (real, synthetic, or absent) are handled, KD routinely yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and when practitioners explicitly address robustness, fairness, and distributional mismatch. However, KD is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the choice of distillation signal determine success, and careful objective design and evaluation are required to avoid propagating teacher errors or amplifying undesirable behaviors.
