papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfers information from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost while retaining much of the teacher’s performance. Across vision, speech, and NLP, KD has evolved from soft‑logit matching to richer objectives that align intermediate representations, attention maps, and relational structure; it is routinely combined with structural compression (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (data‑free synthesis, selective sampling). Empirical practice shows KD delivers strong accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs when teacher quality, student capacity, distillation signals, and data are co‑designed for deployment, but important limitations remain around robustness, long‑tail/rare behaviour, privacy, and reliable distillation without original data.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best treated as a core, first‑line strategy for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students when the method is applied as part of a system‑level pipeline. KD reliably reduces inference cost and model size while retaining much of a teacher’s performance across vision, speech, and language tasks, provided practitioners attend to what form of knowledge is transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is combined with structural compression and data strategies. KD’s strengths are its methodological flexibility (soft targets, feature and attention matching, multi‑teacher schedules, and data synthesis) and its ability to compose with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its principal limits arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and risks of transferring undesirable teacher behaviors; these require explicit remedies (capacity-aware student design, representation projection, multi‑teacher or synthetic data, and robustness evaluation). When deployed as an engineering pipeline rather than a single loss term, KD yields compact models that meet practical latency, memory, and deployment constraints while exposing clear research challenges around robustness, privacy, and automated student design.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is best understood as the practical core of model compression for deep learning and NLP: a multifaceted toolkit that reliably reduces inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance when combined with careful design choices. KD succeeds because it can transfer soft predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and relational structure, and because it composes naturally with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design) and data strategies (augmentation, synthesis, and privacy-preserving proxies). However, KD is not a universal cure — its effectiveness depends on teacher–student compatibility, access to appropriate data (or viable data-free alternatives), and explicit handling of robustness, rare-token behavior, and privacy constraints. Practitioners should therefore treat KD as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines and pair it with targeted engineering, diagnostics, and domain-aware choices to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Default First‑Line Toolkit for Model Compression: Practical Strengths and Required Safeguards
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. Treated as a pipeline—selecting appropriate distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations), co-designing student architectures, and combining KD with complementary structural compression and data strategies—KD routinely yields strong accuracy/efficiency trade-offs across vision and NLP. However, KD is context dependent: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, student capacity, data provenance and coverage, and explicit evaluation for robustness, fairness, and rare-token or domain-specific behaviors. Accordingly, KD should be adopted as a first‑line strategy for model compression while practitioners implement targeted mitigations for known failure modes and validate performance under realistic deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Moran
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used approach to compress large neural models into smaller, efficient students by transferring useful information from a trained teacher. Over the past decade KD has evolved from simple soft-label matching to a family of techniques that include feature- and attention-level imitation, progressive module replacement, self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants. Empirical work across computer vision, ranking, speech, and natural language tasks shows distilled models can approach teacher performance when distillation is matched to student capacity, task demands, and data availability. Practical deployment requires combining KD with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and fairness/privacy safeguards while managing trade-offs between fidelity, robustness, and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Mechanisms, Practices, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring richer supervision than hard labels alone. Over the past decade KD has expanded from soft-target (logit) matching into a broad toolkit that includes intermediate-representation and attention matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or teacher-free variants, and system-level integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. When matched to student capacity, task requirements, and data availability, KD often yields strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs; nevertheless, its success is context dependent and practitioners must combine KD with complementary compression primitives and validation to address robustness, rare-token behavior, and data- or privacy-constrained settings.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Practices in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and other modalities. A broad family of techniques transfers different forms of teacher information — from softened logits to internal representations, attention maps, and relational signals — and is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies (including data-free synthesis and adversarially guided generation). Empirical evidence shows that, when carefully designed to match teacher–student capacity and data conditions, KD can retain much of teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include robust data-free distillation, preserving rare or fine-grained behaviors in NLP, mitigating bias transfer, and characterizing when particular distillation objectives succeed in production settings.

papers_seen.author: Salazar
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring information from large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models so that deployments meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints while retaining much of teacher performance. KD methods range from soft-logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention-level transfer, multi-teacher fusion, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. Its practical success depends strongly on teacher–student alignment, the choice of distilled signals, data availability (or plausible synthetic surrogates), and integration with complementary compression primitives such as pruning and quantization. KD is therefore best treated as a context-dependent component of compression pipelines rather than a single recipe; doing so enables robust, efficient models for a wide range of deep-learning and NLP applications while revealing clear directions for research on heterogeneity, rare-token behavior, and privacy-preserving transfer.
